o: Each passenger books exactly one seat on one flight at a distinct time. A booking is **Confirmed** only if, among all passengers on the same flight, strictly fewer than `capacity` of them booked earlier; otherwise it goes to the **Waitlist**. In the example, flight 1 has capacity 2 and three bookings, so the two earliest (103, then 101) are confirmed and 102 waits; flight 2 fills exactly to capacity so both are confirmed; on flight 3 the later booker (106) waits. Since ties cannot occur (booking_time values are distinct) and each flight's status depends only on that flight's bookings, we can process each flight independently — either by counting earlier bookings for every passenger (brute force) or by sorting bookings per flight by time and confirming the first `capacity` of them (optimal).
k: A passenger is Confirmed iff fewer than `capacity` passengers on the same flight have an earlier booking_time.
booking_time values are distinct, so ranking bookings within a flight by time gives a unique waitlist order.
Flights are independent — group or filter by flight_id and solve each group separately.

a.i: For every passenger, scan all other passengers on the same flight and count how many booked earlier. If that count is below the flight's capacity, the seat was still free when this passenger booked, so they are Confirmed; otherwise Waitlist. This directly mirrors the problem definition and needs no sorting.
s: Build a map from flight_id to capacity.
For each passenger p, iterate over all passengers q with the same flight_id.
Count those q whose booking_time is earlier than p's.
Output 'Confirmed' if the count < capacity[flight_id], else 'Waitlist'.
Sort results by passenger_id ascending and return.
a.t: O(n^2 log n) — for each of n passengers we scan all n bookings; the final sort adds the log factor.
a.sp: O(n) for the result (plus O(f) for the capacity map).

a.i: Within a single flight, the confirmation order is simply the booking-time order: the earliest `capacity` bookers get seats, everyone else waits. So instead of re-scanning for each passenger, sort all bookings once (by flight_id, then booking_time), walk through each flight's block assigning ranks, and mark rank < capacity as Confirmed. This turns the quadratic pairwise comparison into a single sort plus linear pass.
s: Map each flight_id to its capacity.
Sort all passenger records by (flight_id, booking_time).
Walk through the sorted list; maintain a running counter per flight_id.
If the counter (0-based rank within the flight) < capacity, label Confirmed, else Waitlist.
Re-sort the labeled records by passenger_id and return.
a.t: O(n log n) — one sort of all bookings dominates; the labeling pass is O(n).
a.sp: O(n) for the sorted copy and result arrays.

w: In an interview, lead with the brute-force definition check to confirm understanding, then immediately propose the sort-by-(flight, time) approach as it is both simple and optimal. The pure-SQL analogue uses a window function: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY flight_id ORDER BY booking_time)` compared against capacity via a join. Pitfalls: forgetting that the comparison must be *strictly* earlier bookings (the current passenger does not occupy their own seat), handling flights where bookings exactly equal capacity (all confirmed), and remembering the final ordering by passenger_id rather than by booking order. Edge cases worth mentioning: zero-passenger flights, capacity larger than demand, and duplicate timestamps (excluded here by the distinctness guarantee, but a natural follow-up — ask how tie-breaking should work). Follow-ups may ask for the SQL window-function version or for supporting cancellations, which would require a heap/ordered set per flight.
